references.text: David asks that the wicked be blotted out of the book of life, showing that there was a belief in a heavenly book where the names of the righteous are written.
Isaiah mentions those who are enrolled for life in Jerusalem, pointing to the same idea of a book containing the names of those who belong to God.
Daniel prophesies about deliverance for all who are recorded in the book, referring to the heavenly book of life.
God's answer to Moses: 'The one who has sinned against me shall be blotted out of my book.' This is the direct continuation and God's response to Moses' prayer.
Paul expresses a desire similar to Moses—he could wish himself accursed and cut off from Christ for the sake of his brothers, the Israelites.
Paul mentions fellow workers whose names are in the book of life, showing the New Testament understanding of the heavenly book.
Jesus promises that the one who overcomes will not have their name blotted out of the book of life, directly connecting to Moses' prayer to be blotted out.
John's vision of judgment where books are opened, including the book of life. Those whose names are not written in the book of life are thrown into the lake of fire.
Only those who are enrolled in the Lamb's book of life will enter the new Jerusalem.
Moses asks God to kill him if he must bear the burden for the people alone—another example of Moses' willingness to sacrifice himself for the people.
Theological contrast: Moses asks to be blotted out for the sake of sinners, while the psalm asks that the wicked be destroyed.
Linguistic and theological parallel in the concept 'to blot out': Moses asks to be blotted out for the people's sake; David asks that sins be blotted out for his own.
Prophetic precursor and fulfillment: Moses' prayer for forgiveness is made concrete in Jeremiah's prophecy about God's cleansing.
Theological contrast: Jeremiah asks that sin not be blotted out for enemies, while Moses asks to be blotted out so that the people's sin may be blotted out.
